5
A student measures the time T for one complete oscillation of a pendulum of length l.
Her results are shown in the table.
l / m
T / s
0.420  0.001
1.3  0.1
She uses the formula
l
T = 2
g
to calculate the acceleration of free fall g.
What is the best estimate of the percentage uncertainty in the value of g ?
A
0.02%
B
4%
C
8%
D
16%

hints: Notice the table values $l = 0.420 \pm 0.001 \text{ m}$ and $T = 1.3 \pm 0.1 \text{ s}$, and rearrange $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$ to $g = 4\pi^2 l/T^2$.
Recall that for multiplication and division percentage uncertainties add, and a squared quantity $T^2$ contributes twice its percentage uncertainty.
Calculate $0.001/0.420 \times 100\%$ and $0.1/1.3 \times 100\%$, then combine as $\%l + 2 \times \%T$ to see which option fits.
walkthrough: Identify the measured quantities: $l = 0.420 \text{ m}$ with absolute uncertainty $0.001 \text{ m}$, and $T = 1.3 \text{ s}$ with absolute uncertainty $0.1 \text{ s}$.
Rearrange the pendulum formula for $g$: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$ gives $T^2 = 4\pi^2 l/g$, so $g = 4\pi^2 l/T^2$. Constants $4\pi^2$ have no uncertainty.
State the propagation rule: when $g \propto l/T^2$, add percentage uncertainties: $\%\Delta g = \%\Delta l + 2 \times \%\Delta T$.
Substitute values with units: $\%\Delta l = (0.001/0.420) \times 100\% \approx 0.24\%$ and $\%\Delta T = (0.1/1.3) \times 100\% \approx 7.7\%$.
Combine: $\%\Delta g \approx 0.24\% + 2 \times 7.7\% \approx 15.6\%$, dominated by $T$. Rounded to the best estimate this is $16\%$. This is option D.

A.explanation: Far too small. It ignores the large $0.1 \text{ s}$ uncertainty in $T = 1.3 \text{ s}$ and the doubling from $T^2$.

B.explanation: About half the $T$ contribution only. It uses $0.1/1.3$ once instead of twice for $g \propto 1/T^2$.

C.explanation: This is the percentage uncertainty in $T$ alone, about $0.1/1.3 \times 100\%$. It forgets to double it for $T^2$ in $g = 4\pi^2 l/T^2$.
